You should instead seize Baihu and present him to Sun Ce.” Wang Lang looked and saw that the speaker was Yu Fan, courtesy name Zhongxiang, a native of Yuyao in Kuaiji who was then serving as a commandery official. Wang Lang angrily rebuked him, and Yu Fan withdrew with a long sigh. Wang Lang then led his forces to join Yan Baihu, and together they arrayed their armies on the plains of Shanyin. When the two battle lines confronted each other, Sun Ce rode forth and called to Wang Lang: “I have raised an army of benevolence and justice to bring peace to Zhejiang. Why do you aid these bandits?” Wang Lang cursed him: “Is your greed never satisfied? Having taken Wu Commandery, you now seek to seize my territory by force! Today I shall avenge the Yan clan!”

p.src: Sun Ce was furious and was about to engage him when Taishi Ci rode out first. Wang Lang spurred his horse forward, brandishing his saber, and fought with Taishi Ci. Before they had exchanged many bouts, Wang Lang’s officer Zhou Xin charged out to assist him; from Sun Ce’s ranks Huang Gai galloped forth and intercepted Zhou Xin in combat. The drums thundered on both sides as the armies fought fiercely. Suddenly disorder broke out behind Wang Lang’s lines as a body of troops swept in from the rear. Wang Lang was greatly alarmed and wheeled his horse around to meet them. It was Zhou Yu and Cheng Pu, leading troops in an oblique charge and attacking him from front and rear. Outnumbered, Wang Lang, Yan Baihu, and Zhou Xin cut a bloody path through the enemy and escaped into the city; they raised the drawbridge and barred the gates fast.

p.src: Seizing the advantage, Sun Ce’s great army pursued them to the walls, deployed its forces, and attacked all four gates. Inside the city, Wang Lang saw how fiercely Sun Ce was pressing the attack and wished to sally out once more for a battle to the death. Yan Baihu said, “Sun Ce’s military strength is formidable. You need only deepen the moats, raise the ramparts, and remain firmly behind the walls without coming out. Within a month their provisions will be exhausted, and they will withdraw of their own accord. Then we can strike when they are vulnerable and defeat them without a battle.” Wang Lang accepted his counsel and held Kuaiji firmly, refusing to come out.

p.src: Sun Ce attacked for several days in succession without success, and so consulted with his commanders. Sun Jing said, “Wang Lang relies upon the strength of the city and defends it stubbornly; it will be difficult to take quickly. Most of Kuaiji’s money and grain is stored at Zhadu. That place is only several dozen li from here. We should send troops to seize it first: this is what is meant by attacking the unprepared and appearing where least expected.” Sun Ce was delighted. “Uncle, this excellent stratagem will be enough to break the enemy!” He immediately ordered fires lit at every gate and banners displayed to create the illusion that the army remained. Then, during the night, he lifted the siege and withdrew southward. Zhou Yu stepped forward and said, “Once my lord’s main army moves, Wang Lang is certain to leave the city in pursuit. We can defeat him with an ambush.” Sun Ce replied, “I have already made preparations. The city shall be ours tonight.” He then ordered the army to set out.

p.src: Now Wang Lang, hearing that Sun Ce’s army had withdrawn, personally led his men up the watchtower to observe; but when he saw fires blazing beneath the walls and the banners still standing in orderly array, he was filled with doubt. Zhou Xin said, “Sun Ce has fled. He has set this ruse merely to confuse us. We should send troops out to strike him.” Yan Baihu said, “Could Sun Ce be heading for Zhadu? I shall order my troops to pursue him with General Zhou.” Wang Lang said, “Zhadu is where I store my provisions, so it must indeed be guarded. Lead the troops ahead; I shall follow behind to support you.” Yan Baihu and Zhou Xin led five thousand soldiers out of the city in pursuit. Near the first watch, more than twenty li from the city, a drum suddenly sounded in the dense woods and a host of torches flared at once. Yan Baihu was greatly alarmed and immediately reined in his horse to flee back. A commander rode out ahead and blocked his path. In the firelight they saw that it was Sun Ce. Zhou Xin came at him brandishing his saber, but Sun Ce killed him with a single thrust of his spear. All the remaining troops surrendered. Yan Baihu cut a bloody path through the enemy and fled toward Yuhang.

p.src: When Wang Lang learned that his vanguard had been defeated, he dared not return to the city. He led his followers away and fled toward the coast. Sun Ce brought his main army back, seized the city in the flush of victory, and restored order among the people. Before another day had passed, a man appeared before Sun Ce’s army bearing Yan Baihu’s head as an offering. Sun Ce observed that the man stood eight chi tall, with a square face and a broad mouth. Asked his name, the man proved to be Dong Xi, courtesy name Yuandai, a native of Yuyao in Kuaiji. Sun Ce was pleased and appointed him Major of a Separate Command. From then on, all the eastern territories were pacified. Sun Ce ordered his uncle Sun Jing to guard them, appointed Zhu Zhi Administrator of Wu Commandery, and withdrew his army to Jiangdong.

p.src: Meanwhile, as Sun Quan and Zhou Tai were guarding Xuancheng, mountain bandits suddenly rose and attacked from every side. It was deep in the night, and there was no time to resist. Zhou Tai lifted Sun Quan into his arms and set him on a horse. The bandits came slashing at them with their blades. Bare-bodied and on foot, Zhou Tai wielded his saber against them and slew more than ten. Then a bandit galloped up behind them and thrust his spear straight at Zhou Tai. Zhou Tai seized the shaft, dragged the man from his horse, took both spear and mount, and cut a bloody path through the enemy, rescuing Sun Quan. The remaining bandits fled far away. Zhou Tai had suffered twelve spear wounds. The wounds swelled, and his life hung by a thread.

p.src: Sun Ce was greatly alarmed when he heard of it. Dong Xi, who served under his command, said, “Once, while I was fighting pirates, I suffered several spear wounds. Yu Fan, a worthy official of Kuaiji, recommended a physician to me, and I recovered within half a month.” Sun Ce asked, “Can this Yu Fan be Yu Zhongxiang?” Dong Xi replied, “It is.” Sun Ce said, “He is a worthy man. I ought to employ him.” He therefore ordered Zhang Zhao and Dong Xi to go together and invite Yu Fan into his service. When Yu Fan arrived, Sun Ce received him with exceptional courtesy and appointed him Officer of Merit; he then explained that he was seeking a physician. Yu Fan said, “The man is a native of Qiao County in the state of Pei. His surname is Hua, his given name Tuo, and his courtesy name Yuanhua. He is truly the divine physician of our age. I shall bring him here to see you.”

p.src: Within a few days, the physician was brought before him. When Sun Ce saw him, he had the youthful complexion of a child and the white hair of a crane, with the ethereal bearing of one who had transcended the worldly realm. He therefore received him as an honored guest and asked him to examine Zhou Tai's wounds. Hua Tuo said, “This is a simple matter.” He treated him with medicine, and within a month Zhou Tai was healed. Sun Ce was overjoyed and rewarded Hua Tuo generously. He then advanced his troops and exterminated the mountain bandits. All Jiangnan was pacified. Sun Ce assigned his officers and soldiers to guard the strategic passes in every quarter; at the same time, he wrote a memorial reporting his achievements to the imperial court; he also cultivated friendly relations with Cao Cao; and he sent a messenger with a letter to Yuan Shu, demanding the return of the Imperial Seal.

p.src: Now Yuan Shu secretly harbored ambitions of proclaiming himself emperor, so he sent a reply full of excuses and refused to return the seal. He hurriedly summoned his chief secretary Yang Dajiang, Commander Zhang Xun, Ji Ling, Qiao Rui, the senior generals Lei Bo and Chen Lan, and more than thirty others, and said to them in council, “Sun Ce borrowed troops and horses from me to launch his enterprise. Now that he has gained all the territory east of the Yangtze, he gives no thought to repaying the source of his success but instead demands the seal from me. This is grossly insolent. What plan should we use against him?” Chief Secretary Yang Dajiang said, “Sun Ce holds the natural defenses of the Yangtze; his troops are elite and his provisions abundant. We cannot move against him yet. We should first attack Liu Bei to avenge his unprovoked assault upon us the other day. It will not be too late to deal with Sun Ce afterward.
